title: Expect to be laughed at
hook: take up philosophy and some will mock you; hold to what seems best (Enchiridion 22)

segments.voice: Yesterday: nothing to envy, memento mori. Your line was on the same short visit. When envy pinched, did you widen the picture and let it shrink? Day three hundred fifty-four.

You've been doing this practice for almost a year. Maybe you've started pausing before you answer. Maybe you sit for two minutes in the morning, or say a line under your breath at the stoplight. And maybe, at some point, someone noticed. A sibling rolled their eyes. A friend said, oh, so you're a philosopher now. A coworker caught you breathing at your desk and made a joke about it. Section twenty-two of the handbook has a line for this, and it could almost be your sibling talking. Epictetus warned his students to expect it. Today: expect to be laughed at.
screen: `ALMOST A YEAR OF PRACTICE.` → `OH, SO YOU'RE A PHILOSOPHER NOW.` → `EPICTETUS SAW IT COMING.`

segments.voice: First, the warning. If you want philosophy, section twenty-two says, get ready from the start to be laughed at. Many will mock you. They'll say: he's come back to us a philosopher all of a sudden. And: where did he get that superior look? Second, the eyebrow. The Greek for that superior look is ophrys, literally the eyebrow, the raised brow of someone who thinks they're above it all. And here Epictetus turns to his own students first. Don't put on that look, he says. The mockers may be rude, but don't hand them a reason. Third, the holding. Instead, hold to what seems best to you, he says, as someone posted to that place by God. The image is a soldier at a post, not showing off, just staying. Readers who don't share Epictetus' belief in God can still hear the shape of it: a commitment you keep quietly, because it's yours to keep. Fourth, the two endings. If you stay with it, he says, the same people who laughed at first will come to admire you. But if you give in to them, you'll be laughed at twice. He might be too hopeful about the first. Some people never stop teasing. But the second rings true: dropping a practice because of a joke rarely ends the joking. It just adds a new one. So the advice comes down to this. No raised eyebrow. No speeches about your new morning routine. Just keep doing it, kindly, and let the laughter be weather.
screen: `GET READY TO BE LAUGHED AT.` · `NO RAISED EYEBROW.` · `HOLD TO IT, LIKE A POST.` · `LAUGHED AT ONCE, OR TWICE.` · then, large: `HOLD TO IT.`

segments.voice: Choose one small practice from this year that you want to keep. A pause, a line, a sit, a walk. Picture yourself doing it today, in front of whoever is most likely to tease you. Hear the joke. Notice the urge to explain, or to quit, or to look superior. Let all three go. See yourself just doing the practice, quietly, without a raised eyebrow, and then carrying on with your day. The bell holds the time.
Ophrys. The Greek word for a raised eyebrow, the superior look Epictetus warned his students not to wear; some will mock, so don't put on airs, and hold to what seems best. Today's word.
Your line: hold to it. Keep one practice quietly today, without announcing it, and if anyone laughs, smile and keep going. Day three hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Some people who take up a philosophical or spiritual practice keep it quietly, without explaining or showing off, and let teasing pass.

he tells them not to put on a superior look, and to hold to what seems best.
the Greek word for a superior look literally means the eyebrow
he says if you give in, you'll be laughed at twice
once for starting, once for quitting.

fork.setup: your family teases you about your new practice. what does Epictetus say to do?
options: explain it at length over dinner.
keep at it quietly, without a superior look.
fork.reveal: don't put on airs, he says; hold to what seems best. those who laughed may later admire you; quit, and you're laughed at twice.

original.note: Greek, Enchiridion 22: philosophy, the thing the students have taken up.

trapdoor: what you thought: ignore the haters.
what it means: expect mockery, don't give it a reason with a superior look, and keep your practice like a post.
what a scholar hears: ophrys, the eyebrow, stands in the text for the superior look; Epictetus turns from the mockers to his own students: don't wear it.

notes: Review (2026-10-01): cut the hook's 'exactly the same jokes, word for word, two thousand years ago' and the invented 'before they went home'; softened the uncited trapdoor claim that ophrys was a stock image; removed the 'love of wisdom' etymology; 'Many people' became 'Some people' in howItsDone.

ὀφρύς in Enchiridion 22 for the haughty look: confirm.
